passage: Note from the art teacher, Friday. Kashish had a tray of paints that several children wanted. A boy in a red shirt held out a crayon and said, "You can use this. Can I use your paints?" Kashish smiled and slid the tray over. Chetan had been watching from the end of the table. He picked up his green crayon, walked round and held it out. "You can use this. Can I use your paints?" Kashish smiled again and made room. I said nothing and just watched. Mr Ali

qa.q: What did Chetan hold out to Kashish?
qa.a: Chetan held out his green crayon.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling while he watched from the end of the table?
qa.a: Chetan was eager and probably a little unsure how to ask. He learned by watching the boy in the red shirt first.

qa.q: What could Chetan try if Kashish had said no, and why?
qa.a: He could ask another child, or wait for a turn. A second plan means one no does not end it.

qa.q: How does the offer look to Kashish?
qa.a: Kashish gets something back, so sharing feels fair. Smiling twice shows the trade is welcome.

grounding: A child copies another child who trades a crayon for a turn with the paints, and it works.

passage: In the small school in Sangli, Kalyani saw Anjali hand her green crayon to the new girl. The new girl smiled and let Anjali use her paints. Kalyani watched. Later, she passed her own blue crayon to Anjali. "Here." Anjali smiled and pushed the paint box toward her. Kalyani dipped a brush, grinning.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she dipped the brush?
qa.a: She was happy and pleased that copying Anjali worked.

qa.q: What else could Kalyani do to keep sharing?
qa.a: She could offer crayons first to others too, since giving tends to bring giving back.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Kalyani gives her the crayon?
qa.a: Anjali probably feels friendly and glad to share her paints in return.

grounding: A child sees a classmate share a crayon and get a turn with paints, then does the same and it works.

passage: At the Oslo school, Amara saw Lars give a crayon to the girl beside him. She smiled and let him use her watercolours. Amara looked down at her own crayons. When the girl with the paints glanced her way, Amara held out a purple crayon. The girl smiled and slid the paint box over. Amara painted a purple cat.

qa.q: What was Amara feeling when she held out the crayon?
qa.a: She was hopeful and a little shy, trying what worked for Lars.

qa.q: What else could Amara try if the girl said no?
qa.a: She could still share and ask for a paint turn later.

qa.q: How does the swap look to the girl with the paints?
qa.a: The girl finds it friendly and fair, so she smiles and shares.

grounding: A child watches a classmate share a crayon and get a turn with paints, then copies it and succeeds.
